title: who, which, that, where
tagline: Adding one extra detail about a person, thing or place without starting a new sentence.
why: Relative clauses let you give one extra, useful detail without starting a new sentence — Cambridge texts use them constantly in Reading Part 4, and using one well in your own writing makes a short answer sound much more natural.

hook.text: Sofia points at a boy. "That's the boy who sits next to me." Then at a building. "And that's the library where I do my homework." "What about the book you're reading?" asks Liam.
hook.ask: Sofia describes a person and a place using two different linking words. Which word does she use for the boy, and which for the library?

diagrams.title: Join two sentences with who

before.text: I have a friend. She lives in Cusco.

after.text: I have a friend who lives in Cusco.

steps: Find the noun both sentences talk about (a friend / she).
Replace the pronoun (she) with who, which or that.
Join the two sentences into one.

diagrams.title: Who, which/that, or where?

sentences.note: who = the subject of the clause — can't be left out
that is the object here — you can leave it out

diagrams.caption: When the pronoun is the object of the clause, you can drop it — but a subject pronoun always stays.

head: Pronoun
Used for
Example
rows: the book which is on the table
the town where I was born

examples.text: Miss Vega is the teacher who teaches us science.
examples.note: who = a person, the subject of the clause

examples.text: I have a cousin who lives in Arequipa.
examples.note: who + verb, no other subject needed

examples.text: The boy who sits next to me is called Liam.
The book which is on the table is mine.
examples.note: which = a thing, the subject of the clause

examples.text: I like the shoes that you bought.
examples.note: that is more common in speaking

examples.text: This is the phone which Nadia lost.
Cusco is the city where the Incas built Machu Picchu.
That's the school where my sister studies.

use.point: leaving out who/which/that when it is the object

examples.text: The film (that) I saw was fantastic.
examples.note: I saw the film → that is the object, so you can drop it

examples.text: The girl (who) you met is my sister.
examples.note: you met the girl → who is the object here, so it's optional

examples.text: The teacher who teaches us is very kind.
examples.note: here who is the subject — you can NEVER leave it out

watch_out.wrong: I have a cousin she lives in Arequipa.
watch_out.right: I have a cousin who lives in Arequipa.
watch_out.why: Don't use a pronoun (she) and who together — who replaces it.

watch_out.wrong: The book which it is on the table is mine.
watch_out.right: The book which is on the table is mine.
watch_out.why: Don't repeat the subject (it) after which.

watch_out.wrong: The teacher teaches us is kind.
watch_out.right: The teacher who teaches us is kind.
watch_out.why: When who is the subject of the clause, you can't leave it out.

watch_out.wrong: That's the school where my sister studies there.
watch_out.right: That's the school where my sister studies.
watch_out.why: Where already means 'in that place' — don't add there as well.

watch_out.wrong: The film I saw it was fantastic.
watch_out.right: The film (that) I saw was fantastic.
watch_out.why: Don't add it after the verb — the relative pronoun already does that job.

watch_out.wrong: This is the man which helps us.
watch_out.right: This is the man who helps us.
watch_out.why: Use who (or that) for people, not which.

l1.es: Tengo un primo que vive en Arequipa.
l1.wrong: I have a cousin that he lives in Arequipa.
l1.right: I have a cousin who lives in Arequipa.
l1.why: English never uses a pronoun (he) after who/that — the relative pronoun already means 'he'.

l1.es: La chica que conociste es mi hermana.
l1.wrong: The girl that you met her is my sister.
l1.right: The girl (who) you met is my sister.
l1.why: Don't add her — the object is already the relative pronoun (or nothing, since it can be dropped).

l1.wrong: It's the town where I was born there.
l1.right: It's the town where I was born.
l1.why: Where already carries the meaning of 'there' — don't add it twice.

l1.es: El hombre que enseña inglés es simpático.
l1.wrong: The man which teaches English is nice.
l1.right: The man who teaches English is nice.
l1.why: Use who (not which) for people — which is only for things.

l1.es: La película que vi anoche fue genial.
l1.wrong: The film that I saw it last night was great.
l1.right: The film (that) I saw last night was great.
l1.why: Don't add it — the object pronoun is already the relative clause (or can be left out completely).

remember.trick: WHO for people, WHICH for things, WHERE for places!
remember.tip: Say the noun, ask 'person, thing or place?', then pick who, which/that or where — and never repeat it with another pronoun.

dialogue.title: The guessing game
dialogue.context: In class, Miss Vega's students play a guessing game, describing people and places with clues.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: OK, team — describe someone in the room, but don't say the name!

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: It's a girl who sits near the window.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Yes! Now — it's a place where we have lunch.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: The canteen! Easy. My turn: it's a person who teaches us science.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Miss Vega, of course! Now a hard one: it's the book that we read last term.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Was it the one which Liam lost?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Hey! That's the book (that) I found again yesterday!

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Great game, everyone. You all used relative clauses perfectly.

can_do: I can use who to describe people and which/that to describe things.
I can use where to describe a place.
I can leave out who/which/that when it is the object of the clause.
summary: Use who for people, which for things, and that for either.
Use where for places — it already means 'in that place', so don't add there.
Never repeat the noun with another pronoun (he, it, there) after the relative clause.
You can leave out who/which/that when it is the object of the clause: the film (that) I saw.
You can NEVER leave it out when it is the subject: the teacher who teaches us.
